name: Femi Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential; you can tell me what you say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead the renewals desk at Northline Insurance. I check policy changes, correct letters before they go out and take the calls that the junior clerks cannot settle. I have a bachelor's degree; the best part is catching an exclusion before a customer finds it after a loss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the day stays with you after you go home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On Tuesday I found an old flood endorsement that changed a payment, then explained it to the caller. The approved search tool helps, but I still read the whole policy. Jo, my partner, works variable cafe shifts, and we have about four months of shared bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AI Plateau sounds like the search tool we already use for policy dates: handy, not magic. A claimant still needs us to explain why an excess was taken from the payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm relieved there is no big change. Northline's renewal book is holding up and I've got roughly four months of bills saved, though my partner Jo's cafe shifts can vary each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking renewal corrections and use the approved search tool when a policy clause is buried. On the next two paydays I'll add 60 to our joint buffer, and I'll keep my spreadsheet of the cafe shifts so we can see a short week early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about my own desk. The late train home is more of a worry this week than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where has the small search tool already helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a customer thought her flood excess was taken twice. Saving three minutes on a policy search still leaves ten minutes to explain the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the household has a short-pay week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Jo loses two cafe shifts, we'd pause the meal kit first. I wouldn't call that an AI problem, but it's why I still add to the buffer when my own pay is steady.

say: I'd say **AI Plateau** makes policy searches quicker without changing the clerk's job.
I'd keep a person explaining **claim deductions** to customers.
think: I'm **relieved** that renewal work and my own pay look steady.
I watch Jo's **variable cafe shifts** and keep a household buffer.
do: Keep **checking renewals** using the approved clause search tool.
Add **60 from two paydays** to our joint bills buffer.
feel: **Calm** about my desk, with ordinary concern about Jo's shifts.
S0.quote: Saving three minutes on a policy search still leaves ten minutes to explain the answer.
fieldNote: He welcomes a **proven search tool** after seeing it work on a real claim.
His own pay is steady; **cafe shifts** add mild household uncertainty.

steps.text: Keep checking policy renewals with the approved clause search tool
Add 60 from each of the next two paydays to bills savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption can draft renewals and answer simple claims questions, so we should measure the errors before cutting staff. Robots may come into hands-on jobs later, but the changes to our desk start with thinking software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager may hold vacant posts and set the rest of us a bigger file target. I'm good at checking odd policies, yet the cafe and the insurance wage together keep the flat; I could lose overtime if the system handles routine renewals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a month of paid testing on the insurer's approved tool and record the wrong answers on fifty real policy cases. I'll also check whether the appeals unit is advertising a paid senior clerk role; if not, I'll stay here and put the next overtime payment into savings rather than assume a transfer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy would be too mild if my overtime starts going. I'm anxious about a smaller pay cheque, though a measured trial gives me something useful to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your test log change at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missed exclusion can cost a customer thousands, and I don't want a speed target hiding that. I'd bring the fifty-case log to my manager before agreeing to review more files per day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much household pay can disappear before you seek another role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo said we can manage a month without my overtime if the cafe rota stays full. We can't treat that as guaranteed, so the transfer has to carry actual paid hours before I move. I would compare the new take-home pay after the bus fare with our rent and fixed bills first.

say: I'd demand an **error test** before cutting renewal staff.
I'd say **thinking software** changes our desks before robots reach hands-on work.
think: I may lose **overtime pay** as routine renewals move to software.
I cannot **guarantee** Jo's cafe rota will replace my overtime.
do: Test **fifty policy cases** during paid hours and log errors.
Check for an **advertised paid appeals role** before requesting transfer.
Save the **next overtime payment** while it still exists.
feel: **Anxious** about overtime, with a useful test to run.
S1.quote: A missed exclusion can cost a customer thousands, and I don't want a speed target hiding that.
fieldNote: A **measured pilot** fits his habit of adopting tools after proof.
A transfer is conditional on **paid hours**, while household income is variable.
He brings his **fifty-case log** to management before accepting higher targets.

steps.text: Keep checking renewals and log fifty approved-tool errors on paid time
Check paid appeals openings and compare net pay after bus fare with flat bills
Save the next insurance overtime payment for flat bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my branch that AGI by 2028 could handle most renewal checks and customer questions before the 2031 robots arrive. We need a clear appeal route and written notice about jobs, because a customer cannot argue with a blank screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Northline to remove most of the renewal team, including my post, when thinking AI gets cheaper. Four months saved would help for a little while, but Jo's cafe income won't cover both shares of the flat, and I'm awake at night working out the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask for the written severance terms and put our fixed bills on one page with Jo. We'll cancel the meal kit and save 150 a month while I still draw wages; I'll apply for posted claims complaints jobs with paid shifts, and ask the workers' advice desk about income help if the branch issues notices. I would only take a complaints offer after checking the net pay, travel cost and confirmed hours against rent and electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My head keeps doing the sum after midnight: four months of savings against rent that never waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the first month after a notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pay the rent and electricity first, then ask Jo which cafe shifts are confirmed rather than guessing. I would not leave the insurer for a training place unless fees are covered and it leads to a real paid vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an appeal course be enough of a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A human appeal role might last a little longer, though AGI could reach that too. I'd take a paid offer with a written start date. A course brochure is not a second wage for our flat.

say: I'd ask for **written job plans** and a human claim appeal route.
I'd point out that **2028 thinking AI** reaches renewal work before robots around 2031.
think: I expect to lose **my renewal post** and most of the team.
Four months of savings and Jo's **cafe wage** cannot cover our flat indefinitely.
do: Request **severance terms** and list household fixed bills this week.
Cancel the **meal kit** and save 150 monthly while employed.
Apply for **posted paid complaints roles** and ask about income support after notices.
feel: **Alarmed** and awake at night over expected job loss and rent.
S2.quote: A course brochure is not a second wage for our flat.
fieldNote: He expects **his own post** to go and reports broken sleep.
Paid training and a **real vacancy** matter more than a course promise.
His first cuts are **meal kits**, while rent and electricity take priority.

steps.text: Ask insurer for severance terms and advice desk about income help
Cancel the weekly meal kit to cut flat spending
Save 150 monthly from insurance wages for flat bills
Apply for paid complaints shifts only if net pay and hours cover flat bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives Northline time to test a proper appeal system and give clerks paid training. Robots around 2034 are less relevant to policy files than the thinking software in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me move into disputes or compliance, but I don't know whether those teams will have wages for me when AGI arrives. Five years until AGI in 2031 gives me time to test disputes work while I can still pay our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask my manager to let me spend two paid hours each month with the disputes team and use the approved AI tool to compare its answers against twenty awkward policy cases. I'll save 100 a month and watch the posted compliance vacancies; if a paid place opens, I'll interview before taking any course. In the first year after 2031, I would take a paid disputes opening only if the net wage after transport covers our share of the flat and Jo’s cafe shifts are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can make a schedule rather than just count down. Jo and I could keep the flat while I test whether this route is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two hours with disputes teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see the complaint letters nobody can answer with a template. If the disputes clerk shows me how she traces an old policy, I can decide if the role suits me before spending on a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Northline to pay for the certificate and let me study on the clock. If the answer is no, I'll price the course and wait for an advertised role instead of spending our buffer on a guess.

say: I'd ask Northline for **paid training** and a tested appeal process before 2031.
I'd say **2034 robots** matter less to claims than the earlier thinking software.
think: I might move into disputes, but **paid openings** are uncertain.
I need to **keep our rent covered** while testing another path.
do: Request **two paid disputes hours** each month.
Compare **twenty awkward policies** with the approved AI tool.
Save **100 monthly** and watch posted compliance jobs.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to test a path while earning.
S3.quote: Five years until AGI in 2031 gives me time to test disputes work while I can still pay our rent.
fieldNote: He connects the five-year lead to **paid trials**, not just courses.
A certificate depends on **employer funding** or a clear paid opening.
He plans to compare **twenty difficult policies** before trusting the approved tool.

steps.text: Shadow Northline disputes staff for two paid hours monthly
Save 100 each month toward flat bills
Watch paid compliance vacancies and compare net pay and confirmed shifts with flat bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to make claims fairer and plan our own work. Robots around 2039 may move the paper boxes, but the claim reading and customer letters change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still have years to build savings and learn dispute work while employed. Jo and I could clear our small credit balance too, though I won't assume any role is safe forever just because it has a human title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep the renewal team running and use the approved tool for a monthly sample of hard files, with the errors recorded. We'll pay 90 a month off the credit balance and add 60 to savings; I'll ask for paid complaints training next autumn, after the new appeal team posts its actual vacancies. In the first year after 2036, I would keep paid renewal work if Northline offers it and compare any complaints vacancy after bus costs with our flat bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about the next few years. Ten years lets us choose a date for each change instead of throwing away a useful wage now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you check after the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the first annual check I'd show Jo the credit balance, our savings and the number of paid disputes vacancies. If there are no openings, I'll keep testing tools in my present job and wait, rather than pretend the training alone is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a long horizon change any ordinary household plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo wants us to replace the old bicycle before winter, and we can if the credit payments stay on course. That ordinary plan is part of why I want dates and sums, not a grand promise about the future.

say: I'd use the **ten-year window** to plan work and improve claim checks.
I'd say **robots around 2039** follow the earlier change to screen work.
think: I can use years of wages to **clear credit** and build savings.
I still need **real paid openings** even for a human job title.
do: Keep **renewal checks** and record tool errors each month.
Pay **90 monthly** off credit and add 60 to savings.
Ask for **paid complaints training** after vacancies are posted.
feel: **Steady** about near-term work, with a dated plan.
S4.quote: Ten years lets us choose a date for each change instead of throwing away a useful wage now.
fieldNote: He combines **tool testing** with ordinary credit and savings plans.
He waits for **posted paid vacancies** before treating training as a route.
Annual checks will include **credit, savings and vacancies** rather than guesses.

steps.text: Keep checking insurance renewals and log monthly AI errors
Pay 90 monthly off credit and save another 60

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the renewal team, including me, to lose paid posts. Written notice, clear income help and a funded path to a real paid complaints opening would help Jo and me make the rent plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Please ask whether the job people offer after training has wages and a start date. A course brochure is not a second wage for our flat.

headlineQuote: Please ask whether the job people offer after training has wages and a start date.
portrait: Femi leads **policy renewals** at Northline and tests tools on real cases before trusting them.
He has **four months saved**; partner Jo's cafe shifts vary by week.
Steady change threatens **overtime**, while 2028 AGI makes him expect his post to disappear.
With five or ten years, he seeks **paid trials**, saves money and checks real vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens his renewal post before the household can replace his wage.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written notice**, income help and funded training linked to a paid vacancy.
